title: Accessibility UI considers the keyboard, screen readers, and semantic structure together
body: When reviewing accessibility UI code, we don’t just look at the visual appearance; we also verify whether users can navigate using a keyboard, whether screen readers can interpret the content, and whether status changes are effectively communicated to the user.
when_to_show: Let's take a look at accessibility, keyboard navigation, screen readers, semantic HTML, and UI state in the cards.
detail: Accessibility UI is a criterion for determining whether users can actually interact with and understand the interface, rather than just how it looks on screen. We evaluate keyboard navigation, focus indicators, meaningful tags, screen reader guidance, and error message links together. In learning apps, a lack of accessibility can disrupt the problem-solving process itself. Therefore, we prioritize checkability and guidance over visual effects.

title: Analysis and personal information are interpreted in terms of data minimization and the consent process.
body: Analytics code logs data to better understand user behavior, but you must first determine what information is permissible to store. In the context of privacy, this involves considering consent, data minimization, anonymous identifiers, aggregated metrics, and the ability to delete data or opt out.
when_to_show: We'll cover these topics together in the card that addresses learning records, event analysis, privacy protection, opt-in/opt-out, and anonymous IDs.
detail: Analytics code can help improve learning, but you must first determine what data is permissible to store. Focus on the purpose of data collection, minimum data collection, anonymization, consent and withdrawal, and the possibility of deletion rather than event names. For security, personal notes and sensitive inputs should be kept separate from analytics events. It is also advisable to handle necessary metrics, such as accuracy rates, at the aggregate level to minimize the risk of personal identification.

title: i18n reads the string keys and the locale fallback flow
body: The i18n code uses a structure that separates screen text into keys and translation data, rather than hard-coding it directly into the code. “Locale” refers to the language and regional format selected by the user, while “fallback” is the process of safely reverting to the default language when a translation is unavailable.
when_to_show: We'll cover language switching, translation dictionaries, message keys, locales, and fallback languages together in this card.
detail: The i18n process involves separating on-screen text from the code and managing it using keys and translation data. It covers locale selection, fallback languages, handling missing translations, and verifying date and number formats. This structure is crucial even for apps primarily in Korean, in case English descriptions need to be added later. It also takes into account how button lengths and the meanings of technical terms vary by language.

title: The learning UX should lead to review, habit formation, and the next action.
body: Learning UX design isn’t just about displaying scores; it’s a flow that guides users on what to do next. When terms like “streak,” “daily goal,” “review queue,” and “weak concept” come up, we examine how learning motivation and review timing are linked. A good learning app doesn’t scold users for missed questions but instead offers a path to try again.
when_to_show: Let's take a look at the cards that cover the review queue, study streak, goal adjustments, weak concepts, and recommended next cards.
detail: Learning UX shouldn’t end with simply displaying a score; it should lead to the next review action. Features such as streaks, daily goals, review queues, and weak concepts help create a habit loop for users. When reading code, consider the combination of progress tracking, recommendation criteria, reward messages, and retry paths.

title: Mobile UX is evaluated based on small screens, finger gestures, and reading flow.
body: Mobile UX design isn’t just about scaling down a desktop screen. You need to check whether elements are large enough to tap with a finger, whether key buttons are accessible with one hand, and whether code blocks remain intact on small screens.
when_to_show: Let's take a look at the cards covering mobile screens, touch targets, responsive layouts, and code block widths.
detail: Mobile UX isn’t simply a matter of scaling down a desktop screen; it’s about maintaining the learning flow while adapting to small screens and finger-based input. Check touch sizes, button spacing, the horizontal width of code blocks, scrolling, and state preservation after screen rotation. If the reading flow is interrupted, it can lead to users abandoning the learning process. In particular, code examples must be checked for both horizontal scrolling and line breaks.

title: PWAs and offline workflows are determined by cache, installation, and update status
body: PWA code not only makes web pages look like apps but also includes a structure that allows them to function to some extent even when offline. Service workers and caches help ensure fast execution, but if outdated files remain, new versions may not be reflected.
when_to_show: We'll cover these topics together in the cards on PWA installation, service workers, cache busting, offline-first, and handling synchronization conflicts.
detail: The PWA and offline workflow are structured so that service workers, caches, versions, update banners, and offline notifications work together. While caching improves speed, it can leave outdated files behind, so version indicators and refresh prompts are crucial. You must also check for synchronization conflicts with stored data.

title: A recovery design is a structure that allows operations to resume after a failure.
body: Recovery design does not assume that errors will never occur; rather, it is an approach that allows users to resume their tasks in the event of a failure. “Fallback” refers to an alternative path, “retry” means to try again, and “safe default” refers to a default value that is not risky when the actual value is unknown.
when_to_show: We'll cover these topics—fallback, retry, partial failure, safe default, and error recovery—together on the corresponding card.
detail: Recovery design is an architecture that does not assume failure will never occur, but rather enables users to resume their operations after a failure. It distinguishes between fallback, retry, safe default, error state, and recovery action. When reading code, check whether it hides failures, explains them, or routes users to a retry or alternative path.

title: Data governance examines the source, license, and reuse conditions separately.
body: In data governance, it is more important to document the conditions under which data can be used than to simply obtain the data. Being “publicly available” is not the same as being “commercially reusable,” and the ability to modify the data and the requirement to attribute the source must also be considered separately.
when_to_show: Let's take a look at the cards covering copyright, public data, source attribution, open licenses, and derived data.
detail: The core of data governance lies not in acquiring data, but in documenting the conditions under which it can be used. Consider the following criteria separately: whether the data is public, whether it can be reused, whether the source must be cited, whether it can be modified, and what exclusion criteria apply. In educational apps or submitted materials, citing sources and licenses builds credibility. While using data from unknown sources may be convenient, it can increase the risk of legal issues later on when the data is incorporated into a service.

title: The card creation pipeline is divided into the drafting, review, and deployment stages.
body: The card creation pipeline is structured to divide the process of adding a new issue into the stages of creation, review, validation, and deployment. “Required fields” are the minimum requirements to ensure the card functions correctly in the app, while “duplicate checks” prevent similar issues or descriptions from being duplicated.
when_to_show: We'll cover this together in the card that covers card creation, field validation, duplicate checks, the review workflow, and the publish step.
detail: The card creation pipeline consists of the following stages: creation, validation of required fields, duplicate check, human review, and version freezing. As more new cards are added, the generation scripts and validators must serve as quality gates. Traceable steps are necessary to make it easier to identify the cause of errors later on. You should also document which cards were changed in each version.

title: AI tool code distinguishes between training, inference, evaluation, and resource usage
body: When reading AI tool code, you should break it down into the stages of training a model and running a pre-trained model. Terms like “supervised learning,” “LoRA,” “quantization,” “checkpoint,” and “inference” indicate that data, models, and hardware resources are interconnected.
when_to_show: Let's take a look at the cards covering AI training methods, torch/cuda, attention masks, checkpoints, quantization, and inference.
detail: When reviewing the code for an AI tool, you should analyze the sections for training, inference, evaluation, and resource usage separately. Data is input, passes through the tokenizer and tensor transformations, is transferred to the device, and then the model generates the results. GPU, VRAM, batch size, checkpoints, and quantization are directly linked to executability and cost.

title: OCR and document extraction are part of the image-to-PDF-to-text conversion workflow.
body: OCR and document extraction code is a process that converts documents or images visible to humans into text that a program can read. PIL and OpenCV are more focused on opening and preprocessing images, while pytesseract and EasyOCR are more focused on recognizing text within images.
when_to_show: Let's take a look at the cards covering image reading, OCR, PDF text extraction, OpenCV, PyMuPDF, and pdfplumber.
detail: OCR and document extraction are processes that convert images or PDFs into text that a program can handle. Check the input format, preprocessing, extraction engine, failure page logs, and output format in that order. The approach may vary depending on whether the PDF is text-based or a scanned image. For documents containing a mix of tables and images, page-by-page quality logs are also required.

title: Asynchrony and concurrency are structures that determine how to divide up tasks that involve waiting.
body: Asynchronous code is a structure that allows other tasks to proceed while waiting, rather than pausing to process long-running tasks sequentially. `async` and `await` are indicators of asynchronous flow, while `gather` is a pattern for waiting for multiple tasks simultaneously.
when_to_show: We'll cover this together in the card that compares async/await, asyncio.gather, semaphores, workers, and threads/processes/async.
detail: Asynchrony and concurrency are frameworks for determining how to divide and limit waiting tasks. `async`, `await`, and `gather` are flow mechanisms that handle waiting times concurrently, while semaphores and rate limits prevent too many tasks from running simultaneously. It is important to distinguish between accelerating computations and reducing network wait times.

title: Authentication and authorization are discussed in terms of identity verification, tokens, and request headers.
body: Authentication verifies identity; authorization limits allowed actions. Inspect token or session storage, validation, expiration, and failure responses. CORS and preflight are browser cross-origin request policies, not substitutes for identity or permission checks.
when_to_show: We'll cover these topics together in the cards that cover OAuth, Bearer tokens, authorization headers, CORS, and the login flow.

title: Architecture code focuses first on boundaries, responsibilities, and data flow
body: When it comes to architectural code, it’s more important to look at how files and modules share responsibilities than to focus on a single line of code. The service layer groups functional flows, the domain model represents core data, and DTOs define the format of data passing between layers.
when_to_show: We'll look at these together in the cards covering service layer, DTO, interface, boundary, dependency injection, and architecture diagram.
detail: Architectural code focuses first on the responsibilities of each layer and the flow of data, rather than on individual lines of code. It examines where requests enter the system, how they are transformed into DTOs or domain models, and where validation, storage, and display are separated. The service layer and boundaries serve as mechanisms to minimize the scope of impact from changes.

title: CSV and data cleaning are understood in terms of rows, columns, missing values, and transformation flows
body: The CSV and pandas code reads table data as rows and columns and organizes it into the required format. DictReader uses header names as keys, allowing each row to be treated like a dictionary. When you encounter terms like `read_csv`, `sep`, `TSV`, or `delimiter`, you need to check what delimiter is used to separate the file.
when_to_show: We'll cover this together in the card that covers CSV/TSV, pandas `read_csv`, missing values, rows/columns, and rolling means.
detail: When working with CSV files and data cleaning, you should review the file format, delimiters, headers, rows and columns, missing values, type conversions, and storage results in that order. While tools like DictReader and pandas make it easier to handle tabular data, errors often occur with column names and the handling of NaN values. You must verify the data structure before performing any calculations.

title: File operations consider the path, backups, temporary files, and atomic saves together
body: File operation code must consider not only opening and writing files, but also the path from which it is executed, whether existing files can be overwritten, and how to recover in case of failure. Confusing absolute and relative paths can result in modifying files in the wrong location.
when_to_show: We'll cover this together in the cards that deal with paths, folder creation, backup files, temporary files, atomic writes, and safe patches.
detail: When working with files, you must consider the following sequence: path, backup, temporary files, atomic saves, verification, and cleanup. A safe patching script must not corrupt the original file if it fails. It is important to get into the habit of verifying that the script uses relative paths, overwrites existing files, and has a recovery mechanism for intermediate failures. After saving, use `diff` and verification results to confirm that only the intended files have been modified.

title: Refactoring is the process of changing the structure of a program to make it easier to read while preserving its functionality.
body: Refactoring is the process of making the structure of code easier to read and modify without changing its behavior. Duplicate code increases the number of places that need to be modified, and poor naming hides the code’s intent.
when_to_show: We'll cover these topics together in the cards that address refactoring, removing duplication, naming conventions, separating configuration, backward compatibility, and patch risk.
detail: Refactoring is the process of making code easier to read and modify while preserving its functionality. We’ll look at removing duplication, naming conventions, separating configuration, using smaller functions, and backward compatibility. Maintainability is a criterion that asks whether code that’s currently running will remain safe after the next modification. Therefore, patches that change the structure without verifying the results are risky.

title: System concepts are understood by comparing the differences in roles, such as sensors, processes, and ontologies.
body: The System Concepts card goes beyond Python syntax to cover the background knowledge needed to understand real-world systems. Sensors observe values, actuators generate actions, and controllers make decisions based on inputs. Noise, drift, and synchronization illustrate the reality that data is not always clean or received simultaneously.
when_to_show: Let's look at them together on the comparison cards for sensors/actuators/controllers, noise/drift/sync, OWL/SHACL/SPARQL, and threads/processes.
detail: When learning system concepts, it’s better to understand them by comparing the roles each element plays within the system rather than simply memorizing the terms. Terms such as “thread,” “process,” “async,” and “ontology” are also best understood in terms of their position and role.

title: Other runtime product patterns attempt to connect features to user flows
body: The "Other Runtime Product Patterns" card is a supplementary card designed to group together runtime product features—such as Notes, Search, Progress, Save, Performance, and UI Feedback—that are not broken down into separate sub-cards.
when_to_show: View user notes, search filters, saved settings, progress backups, performance metrics, and dashboard cards all in one place.
detail: A runtime product pattern is a card that connects the flow of a user opening an app, entering values, experiencing state changes, viewing results, and continuing from there. Since it serves as a fallback for product features that are not broken down into separate detail cards, it allows you to review input, state changes, saving, recovery, display, and validation criteria all at once.

title: Notes and bookmarks are features that allow learners to mark where they left off.
body: The note and bookmark features are runtime functions that allow users to revisit important cards or confusing concepts later. When terms such as “bookmark,” “favorite,” “user note,” “note editor,” and “auto-save note” appear, they should be viewed not as simple save buttons, but as mechanisms that help users retain what they’ve learned.
when_to_show: You can view runtime product features, user status, search and filters, notes, progress, performance, and UI feedback all together on a single card.
detail: Notes and bookmarks are features that allow users to return to important cards or concepts they’re unsure about. Check the save key, card ID linking, auto-save timing, the distinction between deleted and empty notes, and restoration after refreshing. Since personal notes can be sensitive, it’s safer to separate them from analytics events. If linked to search and filter functions, review the entire process of retrieving information as well.

title: As the number of cards increases, search, filter, and sort features help you find a learning path.
body: Search, filtering, and sorting are features that help users quickly find the learning items they need as the number of cards increases.
when_to_show: You can view runtime product features, user status, search and filters, notes, progress, performance, and UI feedback all together on a single card.
detail: Search, filter, and sort are features that help users find the learning paths they need as the number of cards increases. Check the following: search term normalization, tag and level filters, AND/OR conditions, sort criteria, handling of empty results, and display of current conditions. When conditions change, the page layout and scroll position may also adjust accordingly. Prompts displayed when no results are found are also important for maintaining the learning flow.

title: Progress, Scores, and Dashboards Should Guide Learners Toward Their Next Steps
body: A progress tracker and dashboard are ineffective if they merely show how much a user has reviewed. When terms like “progress tracking,” “mastery score,” “wrong answer log,” “mistake note,” and “export progress” appear, you’re looking at a system that links that data to the next review action.
when_to_show: You can view runtime product features, user status, search and filters, notes, progress, performance, and UI feedback all together on a single card.
detail: Progress, Scores, and the Dashboard are features that aggregate original learning records and translate them into the next review action. They categorize data into the number of completed items, accuracy rates, weak concepts, recent incorrect answers, and cards indicating the need for review. Rather than simply displaying a lot of numbers, it’s important to provide a flow that tells users exactly what they need to review right now. The export feature must also specify the scope of the individual’s learning history.

title: Saving and restoring state keeps the user's workflow uninterrupted.
body: Runtime saving and state restoration are features that allow users to continue where they left off even after refreshing or reopening the app. When terms such as `localStorage`, `auto save`, `debounce`, `state restore`, `settings`, and `user data` come up, examine how the screen state is linked to the saved data.
when_to_show: You can view runtime product features, user status, search and filters, notes, progress, performance, and UI feedback all together on a single card.
detail: Saving and restoring state is a feature that allows users to continue their learning progress even after reopening the app. We’ll look at localStorage, JSON parsing, default values, version changes, migration, fallback, and debounce together. Even if something goes wrong, the app must revert to a safe default, and it must distinguish between settings changed by the user and the default values.

title: Large list performance is evaluated by considering rendering, pagination, and feedback together
body: If there are too many cards, the app may slow down—even if the features work as intended—which can disrupt the learning flow. Whenever terms like pagination, virtual list, large list, rendering, loading indicator, or performance budget come up, check how much content is being displayed on the screen at any given time.
when_to_show: You can view runtime product features, user status, search and filters, notes, progress, performance, and UI feedback all together on a single card.
detail: When evaluating the performance of large lists, it is important to distinguish between the total number of data items and the number of items actually rendered on the screen. Pagination and virtual lists are methods for reducing the rendering cost of long lists. When used in conjunction with search and filters, you should also check the cache, loading indicators, and mobile scroll responsiveness. Performance improvements aim not only for speed but also for a seamless user experience.

title: UI flow and feedback help users understand their current status.
body: UI flow and feedback are features that help users understand what is happening when they press a button. When terms such as “loading state,” “empty state,” “error state,” “event handler,” “click,” “feedback,” and “user action” come up, examine how the screen state responds to user actions.
when_to_show: You can view runtime product features, user status, search and filters, notes, progress, performance, and UI feedback all together on a single card.
detail: UI flow and feedback are read as a single, continuous sequence linking user actions, state changes, and screen displays. Button clicks or changes in input lead to states such as “loading,” “empty,” “error,” or “success.” A good UI lets users know what they’re waiting for and what they can do next if something goes wrong.
